tagline: A battlefield off Back Road, a tannery remembered beside Cedar Creek
intro: Star Tannery Road reaches Cedar Creek in southwestern Frederick County, while nearby Devil’s Backbone State Forest occupies a slope of North Mountain. Off Back Road, Spiker’s Hill marks part of the Tom’s Brook battlefield.
On October 9, 1864, Union cavalry turned on Confederate pursuers near Tom’s Brook. Custer’s flanking movement off Back Road helped rout Rosser’s division.
The northern anchor is Star Tannery, on the Shenandoah County line in southwestern Frederick County. Here State Route 604, Star Tannery Road, meets the community along Cedar Creek off State Route 55.

moments.title: Tom's Brook battlefield
moments.text: The fighting at Tom’s Brook reached both Back Road and the Valley Pike. Sheridan began withdrawing on October 6, 1864, while his cavalry burned barns and mills deemed of military significance. Confederate cavalry harassed the retreating Union forces; on October 9, Alfred Torbert’s troopers turned and routed their pursuers. The speed of the Confederate withdrawal prompted the mocking name Woodstock Races. Custer attacked Rosser’s cavalry along the base of Spiker’s Hill off Back Road, while another Confederate division, led by Lunsford L. Lomax, occupied ground near the Valley Pike. The American Battlefield Trust and its partners have preserved 516 acres of the battlefield.

moments.title: Devil's Backbone State Forest
moments.text: Devil’s Backbone State Forest occupies North Mountain’s slope near Star Tannery. Iron furnaces first drew on this forest for charcoal; a tannery built in 1868 then consumed trees for their tannin-rich bark. By the middle of the twentieth century, little forest remained on the slopes. John and Bernice Hoffman planted loblolly pine and encouraged native hardwoods to regenerate. American chestnut had been a dominant Appalachian forest tree before chestnut blight broke out in the early twentieth century; the Hoffmans also worked to re-establish it. The Virginia Department of Forestry now manages the forest with a research focus on re-establishing American chestnut trees.

moments.title: Star Tannery
moments.text: Star Tannery’s name outlasted its tannery. Built in 1868, the tannery used bark from the forest for its tannin. The community lies along Cedar Creek on Star Tannery Road, in southwestern Frederick County at the Shenandoah County line.
